[Figure 1]

Dr. Sofia Mendoza and colleagues demonstrated that applying mechanical pressure to a copper-silicone polymer composite can increase how efficiently heat transfers through the material. At some pressures, thermal conductivity—as measured in watts per meter-kelvin (W/m·K)—was high (more than 40 W/m·K). But the mere application of mechanical pressure is not sufficient to cause increased thermal conductivity, as evidenced by the fact that ______
prompt: Which choice most effectively uses data from the graph to complete the statement?

choices.A: at 2 MPa, mean thermal conductivity was lower than it was at both 1 MPa and 3 MPa.
choices.B: at 3 MPa, mean thermal conductivity reached its highest observed level at approximately 58 W/m·K.
choices.C: at 1 MPa, mean thermal conductivity was approximately equal to thermal conductivity at 0 MPa.
choices.D: at 0 MPa, mean thermal conductivity was equal to 0 W/m·K.

explanation: Choice C is the best answer because it provides evidence supporting the claim that 'the mere application of mechanical pressure is not sufficient to cause increased thermal conductivity.' The graph shows that at 0 MPa, thermal conductivity was approximately 12 W/m·K, and at 1 MPa it remained approximately 12 W/m·K—unchanged despite pressure being applied. This demonstrates that pressure alone does not automatically increase thermal conductivity.
